en: The Sūtra on the Dharma-Gate of Entering Non-Discrimination,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīlagupta, Imperially Conferred upon as Dharma-Master and Purple-Robed Subject,
Acting Minister of the Court for Honors and Acting Director of the Bureau of Sacrificial Food, under the Imperial Edict, during the Western Heaven Translation Era.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was together with a great assembly of countless hundreds of thousands.
This great assembly respectfully surrounded him and listened as he preached the Dharma; that which he expounded was initiated by means of the non-conceptual Dharma of the Mahāyāna.
At that time, the World-Honored One surveyed the entire assembly of bodhisattvas.

Immediately, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Avikalpaprabha who rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound the Dharma-gate of entering non-conceptuality, so that all bodhisattvas, having heard this Dharma, may practice and study it according to the principle."
The Buddha said:
"Good sons! Listen attentively; I shall proclaim the Dharma-gate of entering into non-conceptuality."
Then the Bodhisattva Avikalpaprabha again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear [your teaching].”
At that time, the bodhisattvas received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said:
"O sons of good family!
If bodhisattvas hear the superior non-conceptual Dharma and abide in a non-conceptual mind, they are then free from all conceptual marks.

Regarding this term "non-conceptual," one should first understand that from the very beginning there exist conceptual marks by their own nature—conceptual marks referring to the two dharmas of grasping and rejecting; these very acts of grasping and rejecting are conceptual marks of self-nature. From this, the characteristics of contaminated phenomena arise;
because of these contaminated characteristics, there are the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*).

The five aggregates of clinging are: the aggregate of clinging to form, the aggregate of clinging to feeling, the aggregate of clinging to perception, the aggregate of clinging to formations, and the aggregate of clinging to consciousness. "Good son!
How does one become free from the marks of conceptualization regarding intrinsic nature?
It means that when no distinct mental attention (*manasikāra*) manifests before one, in this way one is free from the marks of conceptualization regarding intrinsic nature.

If one were to grasp marks as being other than intrinsic nature, this would constitute an object of engagement (*gocara*), and such a state could not attain the correspondence with non-obstruction (*anāvaraṇa*).

Therefore, one should know that giving is formless and without the mark of discrimination; likewise, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are formless and without the mark of discrimination.
Why is this? It is because intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is formless, functional activity (*kāritra*) is formless, and ultimate reality (*tattva*) is formless.

If one gives rise to a distinct mental attention (*manasikāra*) with the desire to abandon the marks of conceptualization (*vikalpa-lakṣaṇa*), then subsequently there will be formlessness and non-conceptual marks that can be abandoned.
In this way, although there is that which is practiced, one cannot attain the correspondence with non-obstruction.
Therefore, one should know the characteristics of emptiness, formlessness, and non-discrimination.
“Tathatā, the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya), and the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) are formless and devoid of conceptual characteristics. Why is this?

Because they are formless by nature, formless in their functional activity, and formless in their reality; therefore, regarding that which is formless and devoid of conceptual characteristics, one should contemplate it as non-different from its own nature, without mental engagement, and free from [conceptual] construction.”
If one is separated from it by means of a distinct mental attention (*manasikāra*), then there will be something subsequently apprehended within the formless and non-conceptualized state.
To be thus is to have an object of activity; consequently, one cannot attain the unimpeded union that is manifest before one.
Why is this? It is because the dharmas attained in the first stage are without form and without the characteristics of conceptual differentiation;
even the dharmas attained in the tenth stage are likewise without form and without the characteristics of conceptual differentiation.
Attaining the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena is also without form and without the mark of conceptual differentiation;
receiving the prophecy of enlightenment is also without form and without the mark of conceptual differentiation;
purifying Buddha-fields and maturing sentient beings is also without form and without the mark of conceptual differentiation.
Even up to the attainment of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), there is likewise no form and no characteristic of conceptual differentiation.

What has been thus described refers to the absence of form by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the absence of form by way of functional activity (*prayoga*), and the absence of form by way of ultimate reality (*tattva*).

"If a bodhisattva, regarding these various attained dharmas, gives rise to a mental attention that conceives of them as distinct from what is attained, as having differentiated characteristics, or as being separate—then they give rise to such distinct mental attention toward all non-conceptual characteristics. Thus, they are not in accord with the principle of non-conceptuality and cannot enter the realm of non-conceptuality."

If a bodhisattva abides in samādhi, their mind enters the realm of non-conceptuality, yet they give rise to the perception of non-apprehension regarding that which has been entered; this is correct correspondence, this is the correct practice, this is the correct cultivation, and this is the correct task to be performed. This is correct mental attention, wherein one abides in effortless conduct without deliberate arousal of thought; this is called the pure conduct of truly entering the realm of non-conceptuality.
“Good son, as for what is called the ‘non-conceptual realm’ (nirvikalpa-dhātu), by what meaning is it named the non-conceptual realm?

It refers to that which transcends all conceptualization regarding all forms, transcends all conceptualization regarding all sense faculties, transcends all realms of conceptualization, transcends all cognitive representations, and is not encompassed or concealed by any afflictions or secondary afflictions; therefore, it is called the non-conceptual realm.”

Within this realm of non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpa-dhātu*), there is no form, no visibility, no abiding, no obstruction, no manifestation, and no manifold characteristics. If a bodhisattva understands it thus and dwells accordingly within the realm of non-conceptuality, they enter non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), which is equal to space. Regarding all phenomena, they contemplate without anything to be contemplated; they attain the practice of great bliss, increase the great mind, obtain great wisdom, and achieve unimpeded great eloquence.

At all times and in all aspects, they universally bring great benefit to all sentient beings. They attain the increase of courageous power and achieve great tranquility (*praśrabdhi*) regarding the Buddha-work that requires no further arousal of thought.
“Good son! It is like this:

suppose there were a great mountain of rock in a certain place, and at its foot there was a great treasure store filled with various jewels—namely silver, gold, and all kinds of diverse gems—and furthermore, there was a great maṇi-jewel that emitted a great radiance.”
At that time, there was a seeker of treasure who came to this mountain, desiring to find precious gems.
There was a certain man there who already knew the location where the treasures were hidden; seeing the seeker coming, he said to him:

"You, seeker of treasure, you should know that beneath this great rock mountain there is a vast treasury of jewels filled with all manner of treasures, and furthermore, a great maṇi-jewel appears there, radiating light."
When the seeker of jewels heard these words, he immediately applied himself with diligence and firm resolve, excavating that mountain to obtain the great maṇi jewel.
Having opened it, he sees that the silver treasure manifests light while the stone remains lusterless.
Having seen this, the man does not conceive the thought that it is a great precious treasure.

At that time, the man who previously knew of the treasure also acts like the former man; he excavates that mountain to take its treasure, and having opened it, he sees that the gold treasure manifests light while the stone remains lusterless, yet this man likewise does not conceive the thought that it is a great precious treasure.
Then the person who knew the treasure spoke these words:
"You who seek the treasure should not strive with such diligent and firm resolve to seek the great treasure.
If you do not apply such resolve, you shall be able to see that vast and precious treasure."
Because of such mental engagement, one cannot obtain the jewels.

If there is anyone who obtains those great treasures, they will immediately attain great wealth and sovereign power as they wish; benefiting both themselves and others, they will perform all manner of deeds universally, achieving complete fulfillment in all things.
The Buddha said: "Good son, because such matters are explained through parables, if there is a bodhisattva who understands this meaning, they will see that meaning exactly as previously described."
The "single great stone mountain" is a metaphor for the single dharma of affliction (*kleśa*) acting in two ways;
the "treasure store beneath the mountain" is a metaphor for the realm of non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpa-dhātu*);
and "the person seeking the treasure" is a metaphor for the bodhisattva.
The person who knows the jewels is a metaphor for the Tathāgata;
the inherent nature of the stone is a metaphor for the nature of conceptualization;
and the act of excavating and extracting the jewels is a metaphor for non-attention (*amanasikāra*).
The silver light beneath the stone is a metaphor for the conceptualization of intrinsic nature;
the golden light beneath the stone is a metaphor for the conceptualized marks of emptiness and so forth;
the various jewel lights beneath the stone are metaphors for the conceptualized marks of the apprehended portion.
"One who mindfully seeks the great jewel is one who delights in entering the non-conceptual realm.
Good son, what does this mean?
If a bodhisattva is able to contemplate according to reality as it has been taught, they will enter the non-conceptual realm."
Furthermore, son of good family!
All bodhisattvas should abide in the non-conceptual realm, just as they abide in the realm of empty space. Why is this?
Whether it be the intrinsic nature of form or its conceptualized nature, when one contemplates in this way, no characteristics appear before the mind.
If one acts with the thought "I have form," that is the characteristic of conceptualization;
if one acts with the thought "another has form," that too is the characteristic of conceptualization.
If one practices with regard to form as having arising and ceasing, or defilement and purification, this is practicing the characteristic of discrimination.

If, regarding the intrinsic nature of form, or its cause, or its fruit, or its activity, or its practice, one grasps at existence or grasps at non-existence, one is practicing the practice of form for oneself;
if one practices in such a manner, this is practicing the characteristic of discrimination.
If one perceives that which is manifested within form, this is the conceptualization of signs.
Therefore, one should know that regarding the dharma of form in all instances—whether as resistance, manifestation, or non-manifestation—not even the slightest dharma can be found;
for this very dharma of form is entirely without manifestation and without intrinsic nature to be observed.
Apart from these material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), there is nothing that can be observed as having the nature of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*).

That matter, characterized by resistance and manifestation, is entirely devoid of observable nature; within that which possesses manifestation, it cannot be observed as having a single nature, nor can it be observed as having a distinct nature—it is precisely that manifestation itself which is also without nature.
This is neither non-existence nor not non-existence; if one contemplates in this way, it is the contemplation of equality.
When contemplating thus, all conceptualizations are entirely without conceptualization; this is the realm of non-conceptualization.

"Bodhisattvas should contemplate in this way and enter in this way; those who enter this non-conceptual realm are entirely without conceptualization regarding both the conceptual and the non-conceptual."

To observe in this way with equanimity is the true entry into the non-conceptual realm; this is called a bodhisattva attaining stable abiding in the non-conceptual realm. It is likewise for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;

for the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—all of which are empty; for suchness, the limit of reality, the ultimate truth, and the dharma-realm; for the dharmas realized in the ten stages, and even for all-aspect omniscience and supramundane practice. It is also thus.

Regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including the knowledge of all aspects—if one grasps at their intrinsic nature, their cause, their fruit, their function, or their activity, whether as existing or as non-existing, this constitutes an obstruction to the knowledge of all aspects and so forth.
If one practices in this way, it is practicing with conceptual signs.

Since all those [qualities], such as the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), are by nature non-representational (*avijñapti*), if there is anything that is represented or cognized, then one is practicing the knowledge of all aspects; this is practicing with conceptual signs.

If those factors such as the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) were characterized by signs (*nimitta*) within the process of cognitive apprehension (*vijñapti*), then this would be the conceptualization of signs in practice.

If one believes that they can be practiced as signless (*animitta*), yet still practices the knowledge of all aspects and so forth, this too is the conceptualization of signs in practice. Therefore, it should be known that these dharmas of cognitive apprehension cannot be viewed as having a nature of identity, nor can they be viewed as having a nature of difference.
This indicates that phenomena lack intrinsic nature, yet they are not without nature.

If, in this manner, one is without conceptual differentiation regarding all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*)—whether in its manifestation or its non-manifestation—then this very absence of conceptual differentiation and non-apprehension of signs is the realm of non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpadhātu*).

All bodhisattvas should contemplate in this way and enter in this way; those who enter in this way truly enter the non-conceptual realm, and this is called a bodhisattva attaining stable abiding in the non-conceptual realm.
At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke in verse:
"If the non-conceptual mind abides securely, It arises from the true Dharma of all Buddhas;
All conceptualizations are entirely abandoned, And one’s conduct attains non-conceptuality."
This Dharma is tranquil, stainless, and supreme; its renown and merit are gathered everywhere.
This non-conceptual Dharma is the highest bliss; having attained it, the Bodhisattva realizes perfect enlightenment.
The Sūtra on Entering the Dharma-Gate of Non-Discrimination Spoken by the Buddha.
